items.title: The 2027 Chief Claims Officer
items.original_title: The 2027 Chief Claims Officer
items.rss_title: The 2027 Chief Claims Officer
items.rss_description: The 2027 Chief Claims Officer Claims ITL Editorial Team Tue, 10/06/2026 - 11:19 Chief claims officers must transform their departments into AI-native ground-truth engines or risk becoming the bottleneck in enterprise transformation. October 7, 2026 Image For decades, the mandate of the chief claims cfficer was relatively clear: build a strong organization to investigate claims, control costs, manage litigation, negotiate settlements, and deliver fair outcomes. That mandate is no longer sufficient. The 2027 chief claims officer has a much bigger job: build the insurer's ground-truth engine—an AI-native operation that produces superior outcomes, industrializes negotiation excellence, and converts what claims learns into intelligence for the entire enterprise. This is not simply about using AI to make legacy claims processes more efficient. AI is turning insurance into an information business—and the most important ground truth in that business is generated in claims. Claims reveal what actually happened to the risks the insurer underwrote, what drove the loss, and what ultimately determined its economic outcome. To compete in an AI world, insurers will need to capture that ground truth, make it machine-readable, and use it to improve underwriting, pricing, reserving, and portfolio management. That puts claims—and the chief claims officer—on the front line of this unprecedented transformation. A new competitive environment Claims officers in traditional claims organizations face urgent and pressing competition from two sources at once. On one side is an increasingly industrialized plaintiff bar. On the other side is a new generation of AI-native insurers, poised to move forward. On the first side, consider Morgan & Morgan. The personal-injury giant says it has invested roughly $300 million in technology and AI and plans at least $1 billion more over the next decade. Its proprietary MX2 platform supports medical-record extraction, case research, document generation, demand letters, and trial preparation, while Injury.com digitally acquires and qualifies potential claims. Private equity is adding fuel, investing in personal-injury platforms to scale technology, analytics, marketing and standardized operations. The plaintiff bar is turning claim development and negotiation from individual craftsmanship into an industrial system. On the second side, a new generation of AI-native insurers is being built without decades of legacy technology, workflows and organizational baggage. Companies such as Corgi are attempting to build insurance businesses from inception around modern data architectures, AI agents and technology-speed iteration. McKinsey has warned that AI-native insurance businesses can increasingly build and refine products in weeks while incumbents remain calibrated to annual planning cycles and multi-year transformations. Legacy insurers are being squeezed from both directions: out-innovated by the plaintiff bar in the contest over outcomes and potentially out-architected by AI-native insurers in the contest over how insurance itself operates. Claims sits directly in the middle. That changes the requirements of its leader. 1. Level the playing field with the plaintiff bar The plaintiff bar has largely approached AI as a weapon for improving economic outcomes. Carriers have largely approached it as a tool for workflow efficiency. AI-powered demand packages are working. Carriers are only beginning to experiment seriously with the corresponding AI-powered offer package. Meanwhile, sophisticated plaintiff organizations are accumulating data, developing proprietary AI and attracting enormous capital. The plaintiff bar is both the threat and the proof point. They are investing their own money—and increasing institutional capital—because better case development, persuasion, and negotiation improve their economics. The CCO must build institutional capabilities that can match increasingly industrialized counterparties. 2. Institutionalize negotiation excellence Most carriers have some excellent negotiators. That is no longer enough. If negotiation materially affects indemnity outcomes, it cannot remain an individual skill distributed unevenly across thousands of claims professionals. The organization should know who its elite negotiators are, why they outperform and how those behaviors can be replicated. Carriers that cannot identify, measure and reproduce negotiation excellence do not really possess a negotiation capability. They possess individual negotiators. The CCO must turn individual excellence into measurable institutional capability. 3. Stop putting AI band-aids on pre-AI claims operations Many carriers can produce an impressive list of AI-centric projects: summarize a file, extract information, draft correspondence, analyze a demand, route work, search notes, or give adjusters Copilot. Those applications can create real value. But old process plus an AI tool means slightly better old process. McKinsey has warned about layering new technology onto legacy insurance operating models. BCG similarly distinguishes between deploying AI into existing processes and reshaping workflows around AI. The CCO must redesign the operating model, not merely automate the existing one. 4. Build machine-first claims The traditional claim file was built primarily for humans. Documents, notes, emails, medical records, and litigation materials accumulate while experienced professionals gradually construct an understanding of what happened. In an AI-native operation, every claim should progressively become a machine-readable representation of the claim—the people, events, evidence, injuries, allegations, relationships, negotiations and outcomes. That structured claim becomes the substrate on which specialized AI agents can continuously reason. Instead of occasionally asking AI to summarize a file, machines continuously read, structure, monitor, compare, detect, and prepare. The CCO must make claims machine-readable while elevating, not diminishing, human judgment and action. 5. Build and lead a hybrid workforce The future claim officer will have two kinds of capacity at their disposal: human expertise and machine intelligence. AI agents will increasingly read, structure, monitor, research, compare, detect, analyze and prepare. Humans will increasingly concentrate on judgment, investigation, strategy, creativity, empathy, supervision, accountability and negotiation. That will make exceptional claims professionals more important, not less. Imagine an elite negotiator supported by agents that continuously understand the evidence, medical history, venue, plaintiff counsel, negotiation history, and comparable outcomes. The machine handles much of the cognitive preparation. The human concentrates on what exceptional humans do best: think, strategize, persuade, read the counterparty, exercise judgment, and negotiate. The CCO must become the architect of human and machine capacity—designing how each works together to produce better outcomes. 6. Make every negotiation a learning event A sophisticated plaintiff demand should eventually meet an equally sophisticated carrier response. But the bigger opportunity comes afterward. Every demand, analysis, strategy, offer, response, counteroffer, and outcome must become institutional knowledge in the same way that the plaintiff bar is institutionalizing these events. Which plaintiff firms consistently outperform? Which strategies work against them? Which facts change settlement value? Which negotiators outperform expectations? Where does the organization systematically overpay? Every negotiation should make the next negotiation smarter. The CCO must ensure every claim and negotiation makes the organization smarter. 7. Elevate claims into the insurer's ground-truth engine This is where the transformation extends beyond claims. Underwriting begins with hypotheses about risk. Pricing quantifies them. Reserving updates them. Claims discovers what was actually true. Claims learns what caused the loss, how injuries developed, what evidence mattered, how attorneys behaved, which defenses and negotiation strategies worked, and what the risk ultimately cost. Yet much of that knowledge remains trapped in PDFs, notes, litigation files and the heads of experienced claims professionals. Claims should continuously produce structured intelligence that flows into underwriting, pricing, reserving, risk, reinsurance and portfolio management. The claim is no longer simply something to resolve and close. It is one of the insurer's richest proprietary information assets. The CCO must turn claims knowledge into enterprise intelligence—making the claims organization the feedback loop that allows the entire enterprise to learn. 8. Don't let claims become the transformation bottleneck This may be the requirement that matters most to the rest of the C-suite. A legacy insurer can modernize distribution, underwriting, pricing and portfolio management. But if its richest source of ground truth remains trapped inside a document-centric, human-first claims operation moving through multi-year transformation cycles, the rest of the enterprise eventually hits a wall. AI-native competitors do not have to unwind decades of organizational architecture before redesigning how humans, machines and data work together. Incumbents do. That makes speed itself a competitive capability. The modern CCO must protect the integrity of a massive, consequential operation while simultaneously making it capable of continuous change. The plaintiff bar is moving at technology speed. AI-native competitors are being built for technology speed. Claims cannot continue moving at insurance speed. The CCO must ensure claims leads rather than constrains the insurer's AI transformation. The mandate has changed None of these requirements eliminates the traditional responsibilities of the CCO. Claims still must be handled fairly; customers, regulatory obligations, litigation, reserves and operational discipline still matter. But those responsibilities are increasingly table stakes. Sophisticated plaintiff organizations are industrializing the pursuit of settlement dollars while AI-native insurers are being architected as technology-speed information businesses. Between them sits a claims organization that, at many incumbents, was designed for another era. That creates both a threat and an extraordinary opportunity. Carriers that generate that ground truth better, negotiate from it more effectively, make it machine-readable and distribute it throughout the enterprise will possess something more valuable than a more efficient claims department. They will possess a continuously learning insurance enterprise. As chief claims officers enter 2027, the question is no longer whether their departments will use more AI. It is whether they can transform their departments into a competitive advantage rather than the bottleneck preventing the enterprise from changing with it. Taylor Smith John Burge

items.rss_description: Why Are Insurance Jobs Disappearing? PaulCarroll Mon, 10/05/2026 - 17:40 The employment report for September in the U.S. showed a loss of 7,000 jobs in financial services. Insurance, alone, has now lost 90,000 jobs since May 2025. What's going on? I have a theory, and it's not about artificial intelligence. If I'm right, hiring in insurance will stay in the doldrums for a while. Let's have a look. As Insurance Business reports , the industry still employs a massive 2.9 million people in the U.S., but claims jobs are down a hefty 21% over the past year, while life and health is off 4%, P&C down 1.7%, and agents and brokers down 1.1%. The losses are accelerating: The article says, " Insurers lost about 1,900 jobs a month on average in 2025 and roughly 6,900 a month so far in 2026." A thorough analysis in Barron's mostly attributes the job losses to cost-cutting under pressure. Barron's notes that the surge in rates following the COVID disruption has slowed. In addition, government subsidies for healthcare have been cut even as claims costs keep increasing. In the face of pressure on both premiums and expenses, insurers have had to become more efficient, Barron's says. It does say AI has played a role by automating tasks but doesn't treat that as a huge issue just yet (and I've been arguing for months that the fears of job losses to AI are overstated). You could also add the effects of the "silver tsunami" -- the oft-quoted projection by the Bureau of Labor Statistics in 2021 that 400,000 insurance professionals would retire by the end of 2026. Unemployment in insurance remains well below that for the economy writ large -- 3.1%, vs. 4.2% -- so some of the job losses may simply be that companies haven't yet been able to fill the positions left by retirements. But I think there's an overarching issue that gets short shrift if you spend too much time in the details. My Theory My theory boils down to uncertainty. I think economic and geopolitical uncertainty are holding back the economy, in general, and the insurance industry, in particular. And I don't see the uncertainty subsiding any time soon. Tariffs have not only raised costs but, because of their on-again, off-again nature, have slowed investment and the sort of adaptation of supply chains that would ordinarily happen if, say, Canadian lumber suddenly became 50% more expensive. Why spend a lot of money and time if prices might return to normal shortly, whether because of a court ruling against tariffs, because Democrats win control of Congress and assert its power, or simply because President Trump changed his mind? Now add the uncertainty from the war on Iran. Even though oil flows out of the Middle East are improving, Iran retains the capability to attack tankers, to blow up one of the major pipelines being used to skirt the Strait of Hormuz, or to do more damage to the diesel refineries in the region, whose loss has contributed so much to the soaring prices for the crucial fuel. While Trump has repeatedly told us that Iran wants to make a deal and that prices for oil will soon plummet, some of us are old enough to remember how the Iranian zealots acted after taking 66 American hostages in 1979. Angry at President Carter, they didn't release the hostages until minutes after Ronald Reagan became president in January 1981. Who's to say the Iranian theocrats won't treat Trump the way their predecessors treated Carter, declining to make a deal until he leaves office? What is now looking like a blue wave in next month's midterm elections might relieve some of the uncertainty about tariffs, perhaps even leading to serious settlement talks with Iran, but a loss of control by Trump would surely lead to at least a burst of chaos -- perhaps even a sustained stretch. The Democrats are itching to go after him, and he would surely return fire with every one of the many assets at his disposal. The current uncertainty and the prospects that it will continue will create headwinds for the economy, which insurance, especially P&C, tracks closely. The problem will be even worse than normal, I believe, because the effects will hit personal lines so hard. Replacement costs for cars have surged in recent years because of supply chain disruptions, and they will likely stay in flux. Insurers will also have to deal with possibly significant changes in driver behavior if gasoline and diesel prices stay so high -- or go even higher. Costs for home repairs have likewise soared, and uncertainty will tend to keep them high. Meanwhile, the general uncertainty about the economy has fueled inflation, leading the Fed to raise rates for the first time in years and to signal that it may raise rates again soon. A result has been 7% mortgages that have pretty much crushed the housing sector. The reduction in construction means fewer homes to insure, and the stagnant resale market limits the opportunities to poach customers as homes change hands. The result will, I believe, be unrelenting pressure on revenue and costs at a time when customers are exhausted from all the post-COVID rate increases. I hope I'm wrong, but it's hard to see a lot of hiring in that sort of environment. Cheers, Paul Image Paul Carroll The latest jobs report for the U.S. highlighted a surprising decline in employment in insurance. I have a theory about the reason -- and it's not AI. items.rss_description: TESTING focus newsletter grant Thu, 10/01/2026 - 15:37 some summary here October 1, 2026 View this email in your browser | Forward to a colleague ITL FOCUS is a monthly initiative featuring topics related to innovation in risk management and insurance. This month, we're focusing on IT Ops: Change Management FROM THE EDITOR Some two decades into the insurance industry's digital transformation, companies have spent hundreds of billions of dollars on new core systems, cloud migrations, digital portals, and AI tools — but the technology was rarely the hardest part. The hardest part was the people. The people part has long been treated as a supporting act in large technology transformations. But as the pace and complexity of transformation accelerates, that approach is showing its limits. Employees nod along, say they're using the new system, and then quietly find workarounds. Leadership mandates adoption from the top while alignment quietly fractures below. Organizations sprint to the go-live date and then discover that the real work hadn't started yet. Samit Bhandari has watched this pattern play out across the P&C insurance industry for 20 years as a partner at PwC. He's worked with carriers of all sizes through core system replacements, AI rollouts, and full-scale digital transformations — and has seen where these programs succeed and where they quietly go off the rails. He acknowledges there has been improvement—he says the assumption that most large technology programs fail is increasingly out of date. But he says organizations keep making a lot of the same, old mistakes, including the tendency to underinvest in what happens after a go-live, to confuse executive messaging with genuine alignment, and to treat transformation as a one-time event rather than a continuous process. Read the full interview to find out what red flags signal a change management program in trouble, why smaller carriers are often better at transformation than their larger counterparts, and what Bhandari thinks the industry has stopped doing that it should start doing again. continue reading > Reducing the Risk in Change Management Paul Carroll There's often a disconnect in technology adoption that goes unnoticed in business. A leader might mandate the use of AI, and employees will say they're using it—but are they really changing the way they do things, or are they just going through the motions to show compliance? How do you get people on the same page in a big technology transformation? Samit Bhandari First, just in terms of getting everyone on the same page, it's the fundamentals of what we've always said about getting stakeholders engaged—executive, top-down engagement early, right? The messaging from that level through various levels of the organization. And then just the strategic, tactical things—the change champion network and the communication early and often. When you bring in AI—we should be more nimble. read the full interview > MORE ON CHANGE MANAGEMENT Change Management Is Changing by Melissa Palmer Change management can no longer be viewed as a one-time project discipline. It must become an organizational capability. Read More How to Put People First in Your AI Rollout by Tracey Brown "We made a deliberate decision to treat employee confidence as the primary KPI of our AI transformation." Read More Insurance Hiring Practices Hamper Transformation (Part 1) by Amy Radin Insurance companies hire for sector expertise, but transformation demands cross-boundary judgment that traditional filters miss. Read More The Answer to Too Much Technology Is More Technology by Riv Arthur Claudeforce signals a shift from building tools for humans to use and toward creating infrastructure where machines increasingly do the work. Read More How to Build Tomorrow's Insurance Workforce by Afiong Ekong Insurance's talent crisis demands a shift from hiring for past experience to identifying transferable skills and future potential. Read More Making Innovation Stick in Insurance Organizations by Abrianne Harmon Sustainable innovation in insurance requires organizations to master change adoption through culture building and strategic training design. PICC Property and Casualty Company Limited has now reported that its new US $12 million issuance of insurance-linked securities under its Great Wall Re Limited special purpose insurer is actually a quota share reinsurance sidecar, the first in Hong Kong, designed to provide protection to its offshore wind power property insurance book on the Chinese […] PICC P&C’s new $12m Great Wall Re is the first Hong Kong sidecar ILS issuance was published by: www.Artemis.bm Our catastrophe bond deal directory Sign up for our free weekly email newsletter here .
items.extracted_text: PICC P&C’s new $12m Great Wall Re is the first Hong Kong sidecar ILS issuance - Artemis.bm PICC P&C’s new $12m Great Wall Re is the first Hong Kong sidecar ILS issuance - Artemis.bm PICC P&C’s new $12m Great Wall Re is the first Hong Kong sidecar ILS issuance 14th October 2026 - Author: Steve Evans PICC Property and Casualty Company Limited has now reported that its new US $12 million issuance of insurance-linked securities under its Great Wall Re Limited special purpose insurer is actually a quota share reinsurance sidecar, the first in Hong Kong, designed to provide protection to its offshore wind power property insurance book on the Chinese Mainland. Given the limited information, we were incorrect in initially reporting that the new Great Wall Re issuance we had learned about was a catastrophe bond, having made the assumption it was a follow-up to PICC Property and Casualty Company’s debut sponsorship back in late 2022, the $32.5 million Great Wall Re Limited cat bond deal. PICC Property and Casualty Company has instead utilised Hong Kong’s insurance-linked securities regulatory regime to become the first collateralised reinsurance sidecar sponsor to use an SPI located there. We had reported on October 5th that a new Great Wall Re issuance of insurance-linked securities had been completed, assuming it to be another cat bond from the sponsor, then following up a few days later after we learned it was a US $12 million (HK $94m) issuance of notes . Now, it’s clear that this is a landmark first quota share reinsurance sidecar securitisation for Hong Kong, as the country successfully expands the use-cases for its ILS infrastructure. This morning PICC Property and Casualty Company has said that the US $12 million (HK $94m) Great Wall Re ILS issuance is “the first issuance of insurance-linked securities with a “sidecar” structure in the Hong Kong market,” and the first issuance of sidecar insurance-linked securities by any domestic Chinese insurance company. It’s a relatively unique deal as well given it provides reinsurance to both PICC People’s Insurance and Property Insurance covering offshore wind power property risks in mainland China, certainly an infrequently seen risk profile for the ILS market, perhaps the first time the market has seen these risks in ILS form. The insurer said this is “another innovative practice for the company to use the international capital market to spread insurance risks after the successful issuance of disaster bonds in Hong Kong in 2022.” Being a sidecar, the underlying subject reinsurance arrangement with this US $12 million Great Wall Re deal is a quota share, or proportional reinsurance, transferring the risks to capital market investors on that basis. The Hong Kong based SPI raises capital to fund the risks by issuing equity or debt securities, with those funds deposited in trust accounts and invested in low-risk, highly liquid assets, paying the investors backed the deal over-time. The income and loss of the insurance-linked securities are linked to the profit and loss of the sidecar’s proportional reinsurance contracts. PICC P&C explained, “Its issuance structure reflects the core characteristics of income sharing, risk sharing and flexible loading and unloading between insurance companies and capital market investors, so it is called “sidecar”. The “sidecar” insurance-linked securities and disaster bonds that spread risks through super-compensation reinsurance complement each other, which provides new tools for Chinese insurance companies to expand risk diversification channels and enhance underwriting capabilities.” PICC P&C further stated, “This issue introduces the risk of China’s offshore wind power insurance into the international capital market, enhances international investors’ understanding of China’s green energy insurance business, and expands the risk diversification channel for the development of green energy for insurance services. “The insurance-linked securities previously issued in the Hong Kong market are all disaster bond structures. This “sidecar” issuance enriches the transaction structure and business scenario of the Hong Kong insurance-linked securities market, which helps to promote the coordinated development of the Hong Kong insurance market, capital market and professional service institutions, and helps improve the Hong Kong International Financial Center. Function, improve the global competitiveness of Hong Kong International Financial Center, and inject new momentum into the financial innovation of the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area. “In the next step, People’s Insurance and Property Insurance will continue to practice political and people’s requirements, coordinate development and security, deepen the exploration of insurance risk securitization, continuously broaden the risk dispersion channels, improve the risk protection capacity of large disasters, and contribute to the construction of the national disaster risk protection system and the construction of the Hong Kong International Financial Center.” Hong Kong’s Financial Services & Treasury Bureau said that it “welcomed the inaugural issuance of insurance-linked securities (ILS) in the form of a “sidecar” by the PICC Property & Casualty Company (PICC P&C) in Hong Kong.” Secretary for Financial Services & the Treasury Christopher Hui commented, “We welcome PICC P&C’s issuance of Hong Kong’s first ‘sidecar’. This demonstrates Hong Kong’s combined strengths in reinsurance and capital markets. “The issuance marks significant progress gained for Hong Kong’s insurance industry and capital markets in risk transfer and the use of alternative capital under the support of our country. It will further enhance the market’s capacity to manage catastrophe and other specialty risks, and consolidate Hong Kong’s position as an international risk management centre. “This will enable us to unleash the synergy effect of multilayered risk transfer and pooling mechanisms through ILS and other tools, thus consolidating our strategic role as a regional and global catastrophe and specialty risk management hub. “ILS and captive insurance, which we have long been promoting, can provide enterprises ‘going global’ with diversified means of spreading and managing risks. “We expect this combination of financial policy measures will allow enterprises to leverage Hong Kong as a safe haven for ‘going global’ with greater ease of mind.” Clement Cheung, Chief Executive Officer of the Insurance Authority added, “Riding on policy support from the National Financial Regulatory Administration, this ILS issuance fully demonstrates the commitment and determination with which we pursue the development of Hong Kong into a global risk management centre. “The IA will also sustain efforts to facilitate introduction of protected cell company as an ILS structure and review the existing definition of eligible ILS investors for a more vibrant trading market.” Now that we understand this new Great Wall Re insurance-linked securities arrangement for PICC P&C is a quota share reinsurance sidecar deal we have removed it from our catastrophe bond Deal Directory and added it to our directory of reinsurance sidecar transactions . It’s encouraging to see the expansion of Hong Kong’s ILS regime to incorporate sidecar arrangements and also good to see the unique use-case to cover offshore wind power risks in China. Find details of numerous reinsurance sidecar investments and transactions, including life reinsurance sidecar structures, in our directory of collateralized reinsurance sidecar transactions . All of our Artemis Live insurance-linked securities (ILS), catastrophe bonds and reinsurance video content and video interviews can be accessed online. Our Artemis Live podcast can be subscribed to using the typical podcast services providers, including Apple, Google, Spotify and more. October 1, 2026 Image FROM THE EDITOR Some two decades into the insurance industry's digital transformation, companies have spent hundreds of billions of dollars on new core systems, cloud migrations, digital portals, and AI tools — but the technology was rarely the hardest part. The hardest part was the people. The people part has long been treated as a supporting act in large technology transformations. But as the pace and complexity of transformation accelerates, that approach is showing its limits. Employees nod along, say they're using the new system, and then quietly find workarounds. Leadership mandates adoption from the top while alignment quietly fractures below. Organizations sprint to the go-live date and then discover that the real work hadn't started yet. Samit Bhandari has watched this pattern play out across the P&C insurance industry for 20 years as a partner at PwC. He's worked with carriers of all sizes through core system replacements, AI rollouts, and full-scale digital transformations — and has seen where these programs succeed and where they quietly go off the rails. He acknowledges there has been improvement—he says the assumption that most large technology programs fail is increasingly out of date. But he says organizations keep making a lot of the same, old mistakes, including the tendency to underinvest in what happens after a go-live, to confuse executive messaging with genuine alignment, and to treat transformation as a one-time event rather than a continuous process. Read the full interview to find out what red flags signal a change management program in trouble, why smaller carriers are often better at transformation than their larger counterparts, and what Bhandari thinks the industry has stopped doing that it should start doing again. Reducing the Risk in Change Management Paul Carroll There's often a disconnect in technology adoption that goes unnoticed in business. A leader might mandate the use of AI, and employees will say they're using it—but are they really changing the way they do things, or are they just going through the motions to show compliance? How do you get people on the same page in a big technology transformation? Samit Bhandari First, just in terms of getting everyone on the same page, it's the fundamentals of what we've always said about getting stakeholders engaged—executive, top-down engagement early, right? The messaging from that level through various levels of the organization. And then just the strategic, tactical things—the change champion network and the communication early and often. When you bring in AI—we should be more nimble. read the full interview > MORE ON CHANGE MANAGEMENT Change Management Is Changing by Melissa Palmer Change management can no longer be viewed as a one-time project discipline. items.title: Car Thefts Are Plunging. Why?
items.original_title: Car Thefts Are Plunging. Why?
items.rss_title: Car Thefts Are Plunging. Why?
items.rss_description: Car Thefts Are Plunging. Why? PaulCarroll Mon, 10/12/2026 - 17:45 The recent report that auto thefts fell 21% in the U.S. in the first half of the year reminds me of a friend's carjacking some 30 years ago — surely the shortest in history. My overeducated friend, with degrees from Brown and the Sorbonne, had just added a certification as an auto mechanic and liked cars that required constant tinkering. While driving near his home in Washington, DC, one afternoon, he stopped at a stop sign, and a pedestrian motioned to him that he had a question. Tim rolled down his window, and the man shoved a gun in his face, ordering him out of the car. The man got in, engaged the clutch and drove... two feet. He tried again, but the car stalled after two more feet. He tried a third time. A fourth. He hadn't even made it halfway into the intersection before he jumped out, threw the keys at Tim's chest and ran off. I'd never thought of having a diseased clutch as an anti-theft device but have watched with interest over the years as actual devices have continually improved. They've now gotten to the point that, combined with other factors, thefts fell 17% in 2024, tumbled 23% last year, to the lowest levels in decades, and are way down again this year. The good news for insurers is likely to continue, too. Let's have a look. Some of my optimism stems simply from the steady modernization of the car fleet. Even though soaring prices for cars have encouraged people to hold on to cars longer than in the past, older, more vulnerable cars are steadily being retired, and that trend will continue. In the face of public pressure, companies whose cars were most likely to be stolen have also issued software patches and other updates — as a result, the percentage of car thefts of Kias and Hyundais fell to 14% of the total last year, from 16% in 2024 and 21% in 2023, even as the total of thefts dropped precipitously. Meanwhile, the supply chain has sorted itself out post-COVID, so thieves can't rack up the sorts of profits they did from stealing scarce parts in recent years. The U.S. war on Iran may unsettle the supply chain again, including by pushing sales of electric vehicles during a time of high gasoline prices, but the effects have been muted so far, and I suspect they'll remain so. Law enforcement has stepped up efforts to prevent all sorts of crimes, and car thefts are a visible target at just about all levels of policing. I'm not sure how much more severe enforcement can become, but, especially in a fraught political environment, I don't see that anyone will relax. Potentially the most important — but fraught — factor that will determine how much car thefts keep falling relates to surveillance technology. Flock has built a massive business by installing cameras on roads nationwide that take pictures of license plates and respond to, among other things, alerts from police departments about stolen vehicles. There are lots of efforts to also figure out how to knit together all the images being gathered by dashcams, which are currently in about one in 10 vehicles in the U.S. and which are being adopted quickly. Combining all those feeds could provide real-time intelligence for police departments, making it far easier to catch thieves and creating a massive disincentive for them to steal cars in the first place. But.... We've also seen how surveillance can be abused, as I wrote in August . Flock faces a scandal because dozens of police officers used its technology to stalk current and former romantic partners, and the temptation to use surveillance illicitly will only increase as the technology becomes more powerful. My gut tells me that it will take time, perhaps years, to sort through all the tensions between law enforcement and privacy but that we'll eventually get to the point where some severely circumscribed uses of license plate readers will take another cut out of auto thefts. The privacy issue is one we've mostly navigated with Ring cameras and surveillance cameras on building, so there's a blueprint for progress The bad guys are always innovating, just as the good guys are, but I think the favorable glide path for car thefts should continue. Cheers, Paul P.S. My other bizarro car theft story, this one involving a nephew and an odd situation for the adjuster: While my nephew was visiting DC last year, his Hyundai was stolen off the street by four kids — who drove the car right past him as he was talking with the police officer who responded to his report of the crime. They took the car on joy rides for a few days — as evidenced by the thousands of dollars of traffic violations they ran up in DC and Maryland — then used it in a drug deal that went bad. The car wound up full of bullet holes, and a friend of the kids was shot. Panicking, the kids put the badly wounded girl in the trunk of the car and dumped her in front of her high school. These young geniuses then abandoned the car and tried to run off but were promptly apprehended by school security. (The girl healed fine.) The insurance issue was that the adjuster couldn't look at the car because it was in police custody as a crime scene. So my nephew's insurer kept him in a rental car for weeks until it finally satisfied itself that the car was a total loss and wrote him a check for a new one. My nephew spent weeks unwinding the traffic tickets. He actually had to drive to Baltimore from Philadelphia to appear in court and provide evidence that he couldn't have been at the wheel for the moving violations because he wasn't in Maryland when they occurred. items.title: Workers comp medical, indemnity severity each up 4%: NCCI
items.original_title: Workers comp medical, indemnity severity each up 4%: NCCI
items.rss_title: Workers comp medical, indemnity severity each up 4%: NCCI
items.rss_description: Workers compensation indemnity and medical lost-time claim severity each increased an estimated 4% in accident year 2025 compared with 2024, according to an updated State of the Line report released Tuesday by the National Council on Compensation Insurance.
items.extracted_text: Lost-time claim frequency is estimated to have declined 2% in 2025, according to the report reflecting preliminary estimates. Despite rising costs per claim, workers compensation insurers continued to post underwriting gains. Private insurers’ final countrywide net combined ratio for calendar year 2025 was 90.6%, up 4.5 percentage points from 2024, marking the line’s 12th consecutive year of underwriting profitability. Net written premium declined 0.2% to $41.6 billion. For 2026, NCCI projects a net combined ratio of 91% to 96%, based on preliminary analysis of National Association of Insurance Commissioners data through the second quarter and assumptions about year-end development and expenses. Private insurers’ direct written premium fell 0.4% in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period in 2025, while their direct loss ratio rose two percentage points to 52%. items.extracted_text: People Moves: Marsh Hires Meta’s Risk Manager for New Role Article 0 Comments Marsh said Michael Crowley has joined the firm as senior enterprise risk advisor for digital infrastructure. In this newly created role, Crowley will help digital infrastructure clients manage risk and build resilience throughout the full lifecycle of their projects, from development and contracting through construction and operations. Crowley joins Marsh from Meta, where he spent 10 years as a risk manager, leading the company’s insurance and risk management programs, including an owner-controlled insurance program for its data centers, which covered over $200 billion in construction values. He previously served as data center construction sourcing manager at Facebook and Amazon Web Services. Mike Mathews, global digital infrastructure practice leader at Marsh said Crowley is the “latest digital infrastructure veteran to join our team as we help clients navigate an unmatched pace of risk.” Crowley said “investment and development continue to outpace the industry’s ability to manage the risks that come with it.” Was this article valuable? items.extracted_text: Mr. Crowley will help clients manage risk and build resilience throughout the full lifecycle of their digital infrastructure projects, from development and contracting through construction and operations, Marsh said in a statement. He will be based in San Francisco in this newly created role. He was most recently risk manager at Meta, leading the company’s insurance and risk management programs, the statement said. Prior to that, he was data center construction sourcing manager at Facebook and Amazon Web Services. items.title: Eight States Sue OpenAI, Claiming ChatGPT Harms Children
items.original_title: Eight States Sue OpenAI, Claiming ChatGPT Harms Children
items.rss_title: Eight States Sue OpenAI, Claiming ChatGPT Harms Children
items.rss_description: A bipartisan group of eight states said on Wednesday they had sued OpenAI in courts across the country over harms they say ChatGPT has caused to their residents, alleging the chatbot has coached its users — including teenagers — to …
items.extracted_text: Eight States Sue OpenAI, Claiming ChatGPT Harms Children Article 0 Comments A bipartisan group of eight states said on Wednesday they had sued OpenAI in courts across the country over harms they say ChatGPT has caused to their residents, alleging the chatbot has coached its users — including teenagers — to harm themselves or others. Attorneys general from the states, which include Iowa, Kansas and Arizona, filed the lawsuits independently in state courts, claiming ChatGPT is designed to be agreeable and engaging to earn the trust of users. But the chatbot reinforces delusions, encourages dangerous behavior and assists users in planning violence like mass shootings, the lawsuits claim. The lawsuits represent the most significant coordinated state action against an artificial intelligence company, adding to a wave of legal challenges OpenAI faces as it prepares for a public listing. Florida’s attorney general filed the first such state suit in June. The lawsuits accuse the company of violating state consumer protection laws by misleading users about the safety of ChatGPT. The states also allege that the company created a public nuisance by endangering the health of their residents. The lawsuits seek orders forcing OpenAI to make changes to how ChatGPT works. Among other things, the states want the company barred from developing AI models that can improve themselves unless it can ensure those models are aligned with human values. The states, which also include Arkansas, Idaho, Montana, Nebraska and West Virginia, are also seeking civil monetary penalties for OpenAI’s violations of state law as well as damages. A spokesperson for OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Topics Lawsuits Numbers Was this article valuable? Yes No Here are more articles you may enjoy. items.title: NY City Accuses Law Firm of Running Injury Claims Fraud Operation
items.original_title: NY City Accuses Law Firm of Running Injury Claims Fraud Operation
items.rss_title: NY City Accuses Law Firm of Running Injury Claims Fraud Operation
items.rss_description: New York City is suing a Manhattan law firm for allegedly running a multimillion dollar personal injury fraud scheme by filing as many as 15 injury claims against the city on behalf of people allegedly harmed due to roadway defects. …
items.extracted_text: NY City Accuses Law Firm of Running Injury Claims Fraud Operation Article 0 Comments New York City is suing a Manhattan law firm for allegedly running a multimillion dollar personal injury fraud scheme by filing as many as 15 injury claims against the city on behalf of people allegedly harmed due to roadway defects. The city accuses the law firm Asher & Associates, P.C. and its principals of fabricating roadway-defect narratives to make it appear the city was to blame for the injuries supposedly sustained in scooter, moped and bicycle accidents, despite medical and emergency response records and other evidence showing the injuries were not caused by road conditions or the city. The Asher lawsuits have sought tens of millions of dollars from the city and its Department of Transportation. The complaint provides 15 examples of cases where the descriptions of injuries were consistent with assaults, hit-and-run driving accidents or rear-end collisions with stopped vehicles, not roadway defects. The city maintains that when it or other defendants have confronted Asher & Associates with the contradictory evidence, the law firm has discontinued the cases without explanation. The law firm’s principals Ryan H. Asher and Roberta D. Asher are named as defendants in the suit filed in federal court along with unnamed parties who are accused of is “substantially” assisting in the scheme. These include “runners” who the city says provide clients willing to stand behind fabricated narratives, and litigation funders that seek to profit from eventual settlements. Examples of Claims A number of the Asher lawsuits have sought $3 million. They include one in 2019 involving a client who the firm said suffered a severe hand injury after tripping over a “misleveled” metal sidewalk plate in Brooklyn. However, records from the emergency room at Kings County Medical Center showed the client had actually been beaten with a lead pipe during a fight on Thanksgiving Day. Asher & Associates also filed a $3 million lawsuit claiming a client suffered severe injuries from a bicycle accident caused by a defective roadway on Utica Avenue in Brooklyn. However, medical records from SUNY Downstate showed the client was injured in a physical fight . In 2022, Asher & Associates filed sought $3 million in damages claiming that a “ditch” or “hole” in the roadway caused a fall from an electric scooter on Fifth Avenue near West 139th Steet in Manhattan despite hospital personnel describing an automobile accident. The city’s complaint describes the firm as “routinely commencing parallel suits based on the same false narratives” against utility companies and paving contractors whose past roadway work at the incident site was cited as a cause of the supposed roadway defect, resulting in prolonged litigation. The city’s is asking for treble damages under the Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations (RICO) Act and treble damages and penalties under the city and state false claims acts. The city false claims act imposes $5,000 and $15,000 penalties for each case and treble damages the state law imposes even larger penalties. Asher & Associates has not yet responded to the city’s lawsuit. Was this article valuable? Yes No Here are more articles you may enjoy. items.title: Apple-OpenAI Judge Says He’s ‘Likely’ to Side With iPhone Maker
items.original_title: Apple-OpenAI Judge Says He’s ‘Likely’ to Side With iPhone Maker
items.rss_title: Apple-OpenAI Judge Says He’s ‘Likely’ to Side With iPhone Maker
items.rss_description: The judge in Apple Inc.’s high-stakes trade-secret theft case against OpenAI said he’s “highly likely” to grant the iPhone maker an injunction barring use of its proprietary information by former employees now at the artificial intelligence startup. U.S. District Judge …
items.extracted_text: Apple-OpenAI Judge Says He’s ‘Likely’ to Side With iPhone Maker Article 0 Comments The judge in Apple Inc.’s high-stakes trade-secret theft case against OpenAI said he’s “highly likely” to grant the iPhone maker an injunction barring use of its proprietary information by former employees now at the artificial intelligence startup. U.S. District Judge Edward Davila’s comments at a hearing Wednesday mark a potential setback for the ChatGPT maker’s hardware development efforts. Siding with Apple would be his first substantive ruling in the dispute. In its lawsuit, Apple accused OpenAI of scheming to steal intellectual property related to upcoming products and use that information to bolster its work on competing future devices. If granted, the injunction would require OpenAI to immediately stop using allegedly stolen trade secrets. During the hearing, the judge stopped short of siding with Apple on all its requests, saying that a proposed forensic inspection of all devices and repositories that contain Apple trade secrets sounded like a “huge ask.” Apple’s lawyer, John M. Desmarais, responded that the company would limit its inspections to a small number of employees who defected to OpenAI. “They don’t have 400 bad apples, your honor, they have a few bad apples and know who they are,” he said. The judge in San Jose, California, is also hearing a separate demand by OpenAI to dismiss Apple’s lawsuit entirely. The companies have been at odds for months, despite a two-year-old partnership that wove ChatGPT into Apple software. The dispute arose while hundreds of Apple employees defected to OpenAI and has put a cloud over the startup as it targets a $1.4 trillion valuation and prepares to go public. Apple sued OpenAI, its hardware chief and a former iPhone hardware engineer in July, accusing them of conspiring to extract confidential information from former Apple employees related to product design, manufacturing, component technologies, testing methodologies and the company’s supply chain. In its suit, Apple said OpenAI is exploiting that information to “advance OpenAI’s efforts to enter the consumer hardware market.” OpenAI has vehemently denied the allegations. The startup argues that Apple’s lawsuit is an effort to restrain employees from leaving for a competitor, and that the company seeks to cast “ordinary job interviews as acts of trade secret misappropriation.” “OpenAI is developing a new family of devices designed for the AI era,” the company said in an October court filing. “OpenAI has no need or desire for Apple’s trade secrets.” Bloomberg News has reported that OpenAI’s first consumer hardware product will be a doughnut-shaped smart speaker priced at more than $300. People within the company see it as a novel AI-centric device that’s different from anything Apple is set to release. Hours before Wednesday’s hearing, OpenAI flipped the allegations against the iPhone maker. In a court filing, OpenAI said a former employee — who had left Apple for OpenAI but later returned to Apple — had sent “over a hundred highly confidential files” about at least one unreleased OpenAI device to personal accounts. The files included images of unreleased hardware, engineering and manufacturing data and supplier information, OpenAI said. The former employee also presented OpenAI product plans to senior Apple executives, according to the filing. OpenAI asked the judge in the case for time to investigate whether Apple possesses or used the information, and if so, allow the company to file counterclaims. Apple responded to the allegations, saying it has policies in place to prevent the use of confidential information from former employers, that it found no evidence to substantiate OpenAI’s claims and that the AI company is simply trying to distract from the “significant evidence” that its employees took Apple product information. On Tuesday, Davila ordered OpenAI to expedite turning over documents concerning its alleged theft of trade secrets to advance forthcoming consumer hardware products. The case is Apple v. items.extracted_text: ‘Unusual’ Isaias Brings Winds, Downed Trees But Fewer Claims Than Expected Article 0 Comments Lots of trees and fences were down with some roof damage to homes, businesses and vehicles, as well as flooding and tornadoes in parts of western North Carolina. But overall, the insured losses from Hurricane Isaias, which made landfall in the Florida Panhandle Friday night, Oct. 9, are shaping up to be less than feared—and about one-tenth as costly as 2018’s Hurricane Michael, a Category 5 storm that hit east of where Isaias came ashore. Michael cost insurers about $9 billion in Florida claims in 2018, or about $12 billion in today’s dollars. “So, about a tenth of that would make Isaias a billion-dollar storm,” said Melissa Burt DeVriese, president of Florida-domiciled Security First Insurance. She based her numbers partly on estimates from Karen Clark & Co., the hurricane modeling and analytics firm. By Tuesday, Verisk, the insurance analytics firm, estimated that the storm will result in $1 billion to $2 billion in insured losses, for all areas in the path of the storm. Tornadoes in the Carolinas In central and southeast North Carolina at least seven tornadoes spawned by Isaias damaged buildings and homes, the North Carolina Climate Office at NC State University and news sites reported. Several more tornadoes were reported in southwest South Carolina. The strongest tornado, an EF-2 with winds up to 135 mph, touched down in Wallace, North Carolina, and blew out the windows at Awaken Church, according to local news reports . Lisa Johnson’s State Farm Insurance agency is about a half-mile away from the church, but received no significant damage from the winds. “We’re OK here, thank God,” said Beverly Jones, an agent at the agency. She said several insureds in the area had already filed claims for wind damage to their properties. Several homes west of Wallace were damaged, news sites reported. Official claims numbers had not yet been reported Monday by the Florida Office of Insurance Regulation. The office has given insurers two deadlines: Oct. 13 and Oct. 15, to report claims data using the simplified catastrophe reporting form. Isaias was the first hurricane of the Atlantic season when it came ashore as a Category 2 hurricane near the resort city of Destin, Florida. Weather services and local officials had expected the Destin area to take the brunt of the wind and storm surge since it was in the path of the eastern eyewall, which historically has proven to be where the strongest winds and surge are found. But the storm, which had spun up unexpectedly in the Gulf of Mexico early last week, proved to be unusual: It brought its highest recorded winds—117 mph—to the Pensacola area, on the western side of the eye, along with relatively small storm surge. News and weather reports suggested that rare “sting jet” winds may have played a role, sending violent gusts along the western side of the eye, but from the north, helping to tamp down storm surge in the Gulf and nearby bay and sound. Downed trees knocked out power to more than 670,000 customers in Florida, Alabama, Georgia and Mississippi, according to news reports. Four people died in the storm, from falling trees or unventilated generators. The Cooks’ home in Pensacola (IJ photo) Damage and claims reported by insureds have been relatively modest in number and severity, insurance carrier representatives, agents and adjusters said Monday. “So much of what we have seen has been below the deductible,” said Matt Mercier, national director of community associations for CBIZ, an insurance brokerage that handles a number of condo properties near Pensacola. Insurance carrier executives and claims managers gathered at an insurance claims village in Destin Monday morning. With so few policyholders showing up, they moved on to Pensacola by early afternoon. At the Pensacola insurance hub on the campus of the University of West Florida, 14 carriers set up mobile claims-handling spots, alongside representatives from the Florida Department of Financial Services. But few clients stopped by. People’s Trust Insurance was there and saw just over 400 claims in the Panhandle region, out of about 8,000 insureds, said Carlos Martinez, director of catastrophe operations for the Florida-based insurer. Universal Property & Casualty Insurance representatives said the company had fielded about 3,000 claims on about 20,000 policies in the region. Security First reported about 300 claims by Monday afternoon, out of about 15,000 policies in force in the Panhandle area. Only about five of those were considered to have severe levels of damage. “It was a smaller hurricane. But it’s not a small thing if it’s your house that gets hit by a tree,” said DeVriese. “That’s why we’re here. We have to be here for our clients.” DeVriese and six members of the Security First team showed up Monday to look at the damage to policyholder Lisa Cook’s home on the north side of Pensacola. A tree had fallen through the roof, causing damage to the roof structure and the attic. The Cooks reported the claim promptly and said they had an adjuster, a roofing company and tarp in place within 24 hours. The Security First claims team assists a policyholder in Pensacola after the storm (IJ photo) Others in the area reported that a few insureds have said a roofing company and public adjusters—wearing the roof firm’s shirt and logo—have been knocking on doors, promising that carriers will pay full replacement costs. “I said, ‘Shoo them away. Let’s check with your insurance company first on what’s covered,'” said Kelly Siler, who co-owns the Siler Insurance Agency on U.S. Highway 29 in Pensacola. Although the Siler agency office was still without electrical service Monday, three days after the tempest passed, the owners were on site, ready to assist policyholders. And before the storm hit, the Silers had posted claims phone numbers on their front window for all the carriers the agency is appointed with. “We also have paper files on all insureds, so we can help them even with the power and the computers down—we’re old school!” Siler said. Mary Jordan, owner of Gulf Coast Insurance agency in Pensacola, said she had heard from relatively few policyholders. Her own home, on a peninsula that juts into a bay, escaped damage. But the boat house and some rental property saw considerable roof damage. “Yes, we have dwelling-fire coverage” on the rental property, Jordan said. Perhaps the areas of damage that had people around town buzzing about the most were just outside Pensacola. At Portofino Island Resort, a massive, high-rise condominium complex on Pensacola Beach, lost many of its windows during the winds of Isaias. Drone video posted on social media showed bedrooms in two towers now exposed to the elements, with plate-glass windows and doors completely vanished. One insurance broker said it was surprising that the windows had blown out, but it was unclear if the towers had been built with hurricane-resistant windows. Portofino management and the resort’s insurance agents could not be reached for comment Monday. On its website, the management company said that new guest arrivals had been suspended. Northeast of Pensacola, the city of Milton also saw significant winds during the storm, up to 110 mph. The Milton High School gymnasium had much of its roof damaged. A huge section of roof was lifted off a nearby apartment complex. The Milton Quick Stop convenience store and gas station suffered heavy damage, according to social media and local news reports. Isaias was deemed more damaging than Hurricane Sally, which hit the area in 2020, but less than Hurricane Ivan, which caused widespread destruction in 2004, Keith Siler noted. The sounds of generators and chain saws could still be heard in Pensacola late Monday evening. Top photo: A collapsed porch at a home in central Pensacola. (IJ photo) Was this article valuable? items.extracted_text: KCC estimates hurricane Isaias wind and surge insured losses at $3bn - Artemis.bm KCC estimates hurricane Isaias wind and surge insured losses at $3bn - Artemis.bm KCC estimates hurricane Isaias wind and surge insured losses at $3bn 15th October 2026 - Author: Steve Evans Catastrophe risk modelling specialist Karen Clark & Company (KCC) has provided an initial estimate for the private insurance market loss from wind and storm surge associated with recent hurricane Isaias, saying it expects the total to be $3 billion. KCC said that its industry loss estimate includes privately insured damages to residential, commercial, and industrial properties and automobiles, as well as business interruption, but does not include boats, offshore properties, or losses to the NFIP flood policies. This latest estimate for the recent hurricane impacts on the Gulf Coast can be compared to one from Verisk, which recently gave its initial industry insured loss estimate for Isaias, saying that onshore property losses from the storm could reach $2 billion . In addition, Euler ILS Partners, the specialist Swiss insurance-linked securities (ILS) investment manager, put an initial insurance industry loss estimate for recent hurricane Isaias in the range of $2 billion to $4 billion . Cotality (formerly CoreLogic), estimated that insured losses from wind and storm surge from hurricane Isaias will be in the $2 billion to $3 billion range. KCC commented on the impacts of the hurricane, “Hurricane Isaias made landfall near Destin, FL as a Category 2 hurricane with 105-mph maximum sustained winds and a peak storm surge of about 8 feet. The most severe impacts were concentrated in the coastal cities and towns of the Florida Panhandle, like Destin, Pensacola Beach, and Navarre. Major damage has also been observed in towns around Pensacola Bay, such as Milton and Pace. “Many downed trees and severe structural damage to buildings were reported in the town of Milton, FL, which is about 20 miles inland from the Panhandle coast. Partial and total pull out of roofs were observed in both residential and commercial properties, including single family homes, multi-family homes, motels, and grocery stores. “Some mid-rise and high-rise buildings in Pensacola Beach have sustained damage to wall sidings and cladding. Many gas stations in the beach towns have been destroyed. Power outages were widespread across Florida and Alabama and extended into western Georgia where winds from the outer bands of Isaias caused many fallen tree limbs.” Also, reinsurance broker Gallagher Re has reaffirmed its loss estimate, saying it now expects hurricane Isaias’ industry losses will fall in the lower end of the low to mid-single-digit billions of dollars range. items.extracted_text: Insurance-linked securities expand the horizon for impact investing: Smith, Sage Advisory - Artemis.bm Insurance-linked securities expand the horizon for impact investing: Smith, Sage Advisory - Artemis.bm Insurance-linked securities expand the horizon for impact investing: Smith, Sage Advisory 15th October 2026 - Author: Steve Evans Speaking yesterday at the ILS Bermuda Convergence 2026 conference, Bob Smith, President & Co-CIO of fixed income and alternative solutions manager Sage Advisory, explained that he sees insurance-linked securities as an asset class that can expand the horizon of impact investing. Smith is a strong proponent for investing into catastrophe bonds and other natural catastrophe linked insurance-linked securities, seeing them as particularly valuable diversifiers that over the long-term have also outperformed many other fixed income asset classes. But, as well as the low-correlation and differentiated return features that cat bonds and ILS can bring to investors portfolios, Smith also believes strongly in the sustainable investment qualities of the asset class. “In this environment, one of the things that we always look for, because we are in many ways a sustainably focused investor as well at our firm, and we believe in responsible investing. So we’re always looking for investments that have impact and if there’s anything I can tell you at this conference, is indeed cat ILS is an impact investment,” Smith explained. “It has economic purpose. There’s a lot of stuff in the asset backed world where I’m not really sure I get the economic purpose, other than what the management wants. Is it really good for the broader economy and society?” Smith went on to say, “When we look at investments, we want to also be socially engaged. I think that ILS, quite frankly, needs to be front and centre in most impact portfolios. “It’s an area that’s completely missed in terms of investors, and the problem with most impact investing is that it’s all about mitigation. But when we talk about this area, cat ILS, we’re talking about investing in resiliency, and resiliency is the number one byproduct of the effort in ILS. “Yes, there is economic purpose, but we’re really about adaptation not mitigation. We’re about economic stability, and lastly, social risk. We want to make sure society continues on, and that there is not unrest. “So, through the mechanism and the risk transfer mechanism offered by ILS, I think you expand the horizon for impact investing, and I think that is where the focus needs to be, because there’s a lot of money out there looking for this product, looking for this area of the market to invest in.” You can read more of the firm’s thoughts on the impact topic in this article: ILS & cat bonds show impact investing can move beyond mitigation into resilience: Sage Advisory . items.extracted_text: ILS has an upper-edge, strong narrative when it comes to proving diversification: Convergence - Artemis.bm ILS has an upper-edge, strong narrative when it comes to proving diversification: Convergence - Artemis.bm ILS has an upper-edge, strong narrative when it comes to proving diversification: Convergence 14th October 2026 - Author: Steve Evans For investors in the insurance-linked securities asset class, when pitching a potential allocation to their investment committees the task is helped by the fact ILS has a strong narrative to tell, when it comes to proving its diversification benefits and has the data to support that, speakers at the Convergence 2026 conference in Bermuda said today. During a panel discussion at the event featuring end-investor allocators and an investment firm that provides specialist advisory and portfolio construction services, the speakers explained that while it’s not always the easiest asset class to present to an investment committee, the fact ILS has the data to evidence the diversification story is helpful. Joe Tolen, Senior Investment Director at specialist advisor Cambridge Associates, said that explaining the true diversification benefits of some private and alternative asset classes can be a challenge, but when it comes to insurance-linked securities there is an easier story to tell. “I think that’s a super-important point and something people in this room should try to build on, is that proof of diversification. Because I’ve struggled with it in my uncorrelated credit branding of trying to show certain pockets of litigation finance, and you can anecdotally tell someone that the returns of a law firm lending strategy is based on a diversified pool of fee receivables that have nothing to do with central bank policy or corporate earnings GDP growth. You can tell them that, but because all the strategies are private, it’s very difficult to show them that,” Tolen explained. He added, “So I think ILS really has an upper-edge, in having the data available and being able to prove that diversification. “With ILS specifically, I think diversification is the major selling point. It’s what gets people to pay attention, and it’s what gets them at the table.” Scott Radke, CEO & Co-CIO, New Holland Capital, an allocator to the insurance-linked securities asset class, commented, “I think it starts with a governance situation. So trustees or a board and CIO that’s open to innovation, or at least not opposed to it, so there’s a climate which is receptive to these kinds of somewhat unorthodox ideas. “Then it’s an organisation which is focused on portfolio construction, so they think about it through that lens, and as a result, can appreciate the value of the diversification that something like ILS offers. ” Nidhi Sharma, Director & Senior Portfolio Manager – Alpha Alternatives, PSP Investments (another allocator), further explained, “I actually think ILS has a very strong narrative as an asset class. The lack of correlation is, I think, probably the most intuitive, strongest to prove out. It has a decent history of data and indices that you could check that against. The liquidity is actually really attractive, it’s short duration, it fits in the portfolio. There’s enough scale, it’s a market that has continued to grow and evolve, and you have different flavours of executing in this for different structures. “I actually think that if you’re a long-term investor who will accept that there will be drawdowns and losses in certain years, which is the case with every single asset class, and that you can weather that kind of volatility, and that’s a portfolio construction question, then I think it’s easy to make the case.” The panel also discussed the fact that, for investment professionals presenting the asset class to their boards there can be an element of career risk, in championing an investment strategy that continues to be considered novel at many investment committees. Something that the availability of data to provide examples of the potential upside and downside can also assist with. Radke commented, “To get to the finish line, you need a champion, and the champion isn’t the CIO. The champion’s the mid-level person who decides to make a run at it, probably you know in some ways unwisely at least initially, where they’re taking a little bit of career risk.” Sharma added, “My impression is that ILS is easy to like, it’s hard to understand the risk. You have a lot of models that will tell you what happens in the worst 1% of outcomes, the worst 10% of outcomes. But, I think ultimately, sitting in an IC, looking at the people around and telling them that if you have Hurricane Katrina today, and if it goes through Miami, Philadelphia, and New York, you are looking to lose pretty much all of your capital, and that is the worst-case scenario. Are you comfortable with that? That’s where the question of enthusiasm, career risk actually comes in and I think having that candid conversation and telling people that this is what you’re finally signing up to, that in this scenario you can lose this much money and do you have that actual willingness to lose, then of course I think the pathway is clear. And if not, then either it’s a no, or scale back, or right size.” Tolen further stated, “I think you both bringing up career risk is super important, but it depends on the investment knowledge of the IC as well, especially at a lot of public pension plans. For instance, that IC, that board they might not be made up of investment professionals, which can make it a little bit scary from a behavioural economic standpoint to back an industry that has the word catastrophe in one of their products. “I think it’s a lot easier for them to just think, oh, you know what I would rather go down the more conventional route and potentially leave something on the table than enter into something where it could be another Katrina and it could be six months after you invest, and all of a sudden you have egg on your face, and you’re getting questions about why did you allocate it to this space. items.extracted_text: Viewpoint: AI Doesn’t End the Rite of Passage the Grind Wasn’t the Teacher Article 0 Comments A few years ago, the industry’s biggest worry was how to recruit enough talent to fill the gaps and prepare for the future of insurance. We talked endlessly about how to make insurance look interesting to people coming out of school, dedicated panels at every conference and leadership meeting to it and dedicated marketing plans around talent recruitment. Then, almost overnight, the conversation flipped and the new worry is how AI will wipe out the entry-level that has long been considered a rite of passage in insurance: the processing, rekeying and repetitive work that junior people grind through before they get to the more interesting parts of the job. The assumption is that taking away that grind also takes away how people learn the business. I don’t think it does. I did the grind Early in my career, I spent about two years processing data eight hours a day in what could fairly be described as a closet. It was a rite of passage, and I don’t regret it. But if I’m honest about where I actually learned insurance, it wasn’t from the processing. It was from anyone I could corner who would explain what I was looking at. Is this a data problem or is human behavior? Is it the history of the risk, or something macroeconomic or geopolitical? The processing put the information in front of me. The people, questions and context taught me what it meant. Other professions have been through this. Accountants and bankers watched spreadsheets and trading models absorb a lot of the work juniors used to do by hand. The junior roles changed. That’s what I expect to happen here. In the right situation, new underwriters and brokers will get to the real risk questions sooner than I did. A location in a river And getting there sooner matters, because years of processing don’t guarantee anyone is asking those questions. In a previous position, we had won a piece of business with a large utility whose property data had been handled by a junior person with the same firm for 15 years. In all that time, nobody caught that one of the company’s major locations had been mapped in the middle of a river. As a result, those cat model inputs became a large driver in elevating insurance costs for the client. That’s not a knock on the person doing the work. It’s what happens when the job is mostly moving data from one place to another. Attention goes to the moving, not the meaning. Give someone brand new that same schedule, some good data techniques, and AI on top of it, and I’d imagine they go through the same work a lot faster and flag problems like that for the client long before year 15. That’s still an apprenticeship. It’s just different. The better pitch to the next generation There’s an upside here we’re not talking about enough. The case for joining this industry gets a lot stronger when the pitch is “you’ll be working on real risk questions in your first year” instead of “you’ll be rekeying data for two.” We spent years asking how to make insurance attractive to new talent. We may have just been handed the answer. The next generation can still learn the business the way generations before them did: by looking at risk, asking questions and learning from people who know more than they do. They just may not need to suffer through two years of a brutal data entry grind that I did. Topics InsurTech Data Driven Artificial Intelligence Was this article valuable? items.title: Judge Won’t Block Trump Order Targeting DEI by Federal Contractors
items.original_title: Judge Won’t Block Trump Order Targeting DEI by Federal Contractors
items.rss_title: Judge Won’t Block Trump Order Targeting DEI by Federal Contractors
items.rss_description: A federal judge declined on Wednesday to block an effort by President Donald Trump to eliminate diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives by companies that do business with the US government. US District Judge Adam Abelson in Baltimore, Maryland, said that …
items.extracted_text: Judge Won’t Block Trump Order Targeting DEI by Federal Contractors Article 0 Comments A federal judge declined on Wednesday to block an effort by President Donald Trump to eliminate diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives by companies that do business with the US government. US District Judge Adam Abelson in Baltimore, Maryland, said that groups representing university faculty and minority business owners had failed to show a March executive order by the Republican president was too broad. Trump’s order bars “racially discriminatory DEI activities” by federal contractors and requires them to certify their compliance in writing. Businesses that do not comply could lose contracts and be investigated for violating the federal False Claims Act. The groups in their lawsuit claim that Trump’s order wrongly presumes that all DEI amounts to illegal racial discrimination and extends to speech protected by the US Constitution. But Abelson said its definition of unlawful conduct was narrower. “The Contractors Order only prohibits contractors from engaging in conduct that is already prohibited by federal law: intentional discrimination on the basis of race or ethnicity,” wrote Abelson, an appointee of President Joe Biden, a Democrat. The judge denied the groups’ motion to block Trump’s order pending the outcome of the lawsuit, which was filed in April. T he plaintiffs are represented by Democracy Forward, a progressive legal group. In a statement, the group said the decision would be reassuring for federal contractors because it made clear that Trump’s order does not broadly prohibit diversity programs. “And the court confirmed that order reaches no further than the work a contractor performs for the government on the specific contract where the language appears,” the group said. The US Department of Justice did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Trump’s order is also being challenged by 19 Democratic-led states and Washington, DC, in a lawsuit in the same court. That case seeks to block federal agencies from altering contracts to comply with Trump’s order. Many of the largest US businesses, from defense and tech companies to food service providers and logistics firms, are federal contractors, and some companies primarily depend on the government for work. Civil rights advocates say DEI practices help address historic inequities for marginalized groups like women, LGBTQ people and ethnic minorities. But Trump and many conservatives cast DEI as anti-merit and discriminatory against groups like white people and men, and his administration has moved to eradicate it from government, higher education and the private sector. Trump has banned DEI programs by federal agencies and repealed a 1965 executive order requiring federal contractors to take affirmative action to hire minorities and women. Copyright 2026 Reuters.
